course_description:
Evolutionary biology is the study of the origin, maintenance and diversity of life on Earth. The study of evolutionary biology allows us not only to explore and infer the relationships among all life that has ever lived and to track the diversity of life across vast stretches of time, but also to test hypotheses through a rigorous combination of observation and experimental manipulations.

Much of the biological world only comes into clear focus when viewed through the lens of evolution. BIOL2201 covers the fundamentals of evolutionary biology, from recognising and interpreting evolutionary patterns and to understanding the processes that are thought to drive evolutionary change. We will examine the history and development of evolutionary theory and explore the nature of evolutionary processes, on both micro and macro scales, using a range of organisms from bacteria through to metazoans (plants and animals).

course_aims: This course considers the cascade of evolutionary transitions and associated environmental changes and challenges that have faced life on earth since cells first evolved and consequently gave rise to complex, multi-cellular organisms. The various evolutionary processes that contribute to change are considered in relation to organisms ranging from bacteria through to various plants and vertebrates. More specifically, human evolution is explored with reference to this background and in relation to the evolution of language, disease and modern medicine. An appreciation of evolution should help you to see every biological discipline in a new light.

learning_outcomes.description: Understand how and why evolution is an organising principle in the biological sciences.
Know the major evolutionary transitions that have taken place in the history of life, since the evolution of the prokaryotic cell until the present.
Appreciate how the environment is crucial to sustaining life and forcing evolutionary change.
Understand the various processes that contribute to evolutionary change, and how they operate.
Understand the evolutionary history of modern humans, their languages and diseases.
Appreciate the role of the primary literature in developing an understanding of evolutionary biology, and learn how to synthesise ideas from different sources.
Appreciate the nature of the scientific evidence that informs scientific interpretation, and how evidence is gathered and analysed

assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
Worksheets for each practical class that form part of the Selection Experiments are to be completed in class and submitted at the end of class.
Deferral or extension
You cannot defer or apply for an extension for this assessment.
As this assessment is completed in the Practicals, and involve lab components that cannot be re-set, no extensions are available for this assessment item. If you are unable to attend the Practicals due to exceptional circumstances, please contact the Course Coordinator to discuss alternative assessment. The best two of the three worksheets will contribute to the overall mark, so you may miss one experiment without reason.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
You are required to submit assessable items on time. If you fail to meet the submission deadline for any assessment item, then 10% of the maximum possible mark for the assessment item (the assessment ‘marked from’ value) will be deducted as a late penalty for every day (or part day) late after the due date.
For example, if you submit your assignment 1 hour late, you will be penalised 10%; if your assignment is 24.5 hours late, you will be penalised 20% (because it is late by one 24-hour period plus part of another 24-hour period).

assessment_details.task_description: The Book Club requires students to read a set popular book about evolution. In class, students work in pairs and small groups to discuss aspects of the book and build a set of written responses. They will need to pose a question the book raises, weigh the evidence, and defend an argument. Book Club will take place over Week 4 and Week 5 Practicals. During week 1 of Book Club, each group will focus on a different chapter of the book, assigned to them at the start of the class, and work through a set of activities. During week 2 of Book Club, students will complete a worksheet that covers broader concepts developed across multiple chapters, to be submitted at the end of the second practical. The worksheet will be worth 15% of the course. The task develops your ability to work in small groups and to discuss and communicate complex ideas critically, and clearly.
